# Simulation Reading List

Here is a reading list on designing and conducting Monte Carlo simulation studies for quantitative sciences. These articles are divided into two sections: methods articles, which describe, in whole or in part, how to conduct Monte Carlo simulations; and three published simulation studies that evaluate the performance of different methods.

## Simulation Methods


This article by Boulesteix and colleagues outlines some considerations around doing simulation studies in the health sciences. The authors also conduct an actual simulation study and provide R code that can be used to reproduce their results: https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/10/12/e039921

This article by Morris and colleagues is quickly becoming the standard reference on designing and implementing simulation studies in quantitative sciences:  https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/sim.8086

This article by Koehler and colleagues discusses specific strategies for estimating Monte Carlo error, minimizing it, and using it to select an appropriate Monte Carlo sample size: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1198/tast.2009.0030


This book by Efron and Hastie, though not explicitly about Monte Carlo simulation, presents several concepts and code that are directly related to key statistical principles that should govern decisions around conducting Monte Carlo simulations: Efron B, Hastie T. Computer Age Statistical Inference. Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press; 2016.

## Simulation Examples

Here are three examples of simulation studies conducted towards specific ends.

This article by Graves and colleagues focuses on problems that can arise with inappropriate uses of p-values, particularly in smaller samples: Graves N, Barnett AG, Burn E, Cook D. Smaller clinical trials for decision making; a case study to show p-values are costly. F1000Research 2018;7:1176. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9555245/

This article by Naimi and colleagues evaluates and compares different methods for constructing inverse probability weights for continuous exposures: Naimi AI, Moodie EEM, Auger N, Kaufman JS. Constructing inverse probability weights for continuous exposures: a comparison of methods. Epidemiology 2014;25(2):292-299. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24487212/

This article by Westreich and colleagues presents a simulation study of the performance of inverse probability weighted Cox proportional hazards regression models. Of particular note, this simulation deploys an interesting and unique method to estimate the convergence rate of an estimator in different settings: Westreich D, Cole SR, Schisterman EF, Platt RW. A simulation study of finite-sample properties of marginal structural Cox proportional hazards models. Statistics in Medicine 2012;31(19):2098-2109. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22492660/
